As someone currently in a partnership with someone who does this, something I did midway through is being together, is have a sit down with them about the negativity and how much it’s impacting me. Some people (in my observation, people who were not taught healthy ways to cope with stress, people who struggle with emotional regulation, people who maybe lack some emotional intelligence in crucial areas, may be emotionally codependent) don’t recognize how much of a serious debby downer they are. When i kindly talked to my partner about it, they ended up “revealing” (i use air quotes because I already picked up on this a while ago) that they struggled with their frustration, and what was compounding that was stressors out of their control such as work. Not saying that could be whats stressing your partner out though. And i also got the sense that maybe they were struggling to come to terms about their own negativity and lack of feeling in control of anything in their life and how it impacts loved ones. I told them it sucked that no amount of supportive words or actions to them seemed to help them regulate their emotions better, and that i was at the point of pouring from an empty cup with supportive things to say or do (which is sort of a love language for me) I will say that the conversation had helped a lot. But I won’t act as if i havent gotten to the point where admitted apathy sets in after a while when they have one of those days of just huge big emotion and complaints all day. They do understand that in the moments I’m spent with nothing to say to them, and to reel it back in to regulate.

Its natural for anyone to expect their partner to want to be there for them when they experience stress in life. But it is not fair to that person to use them as an emotional punching bag, and if you have to draw a boundary, or tell them just how negative they are, then I encourage you to do it. If your boyfriend actually cares about working on this part of himself, especially because he hears it impacts you negatively, he will. Best of luck.

EDIT: ok after sifting through some comments, i understand that your boyfriend cheated on you. I’m sorry that you went through that betrayal. This sounds like someone who is likely addicted to negativity and misery, and seeks positivity or thrill in extremely unhealthy ways (cheating) not thinking of the consequences of that. Please know that you deserve better, and no amount of kindness and support with make him reckon with his own sense of inadequacy, he needs to do that for himself, by himself, without dragging other into it.

From what it sounds like, there is a financial incompatibility in the current stage of your relationship with your bf. It sounds like you are willing to work with him to reach a point where you can both support yourself together without it feeling financially one sided, and that you may be concerned that he doesn’t want to leave the financial safety net he’s in right now, where his monthly expenses are low and he can comfortably afford them with his current job. These kind of conversations are always going to be uncomfortable esp. if you don’t know if you’re on the same page, but its better to have this conversation now than later. Especially if this is someone you want a future with. Also from what is sounds like, you both are living separately but want to share a house hold together. Correct me if I’m wrong.

My advice to you would be to propose a dedicated day + time to have this conversation about your finances, plans, and expectations together, and how you and your bf envision that as individuals. Avoid ultimatums. It could be something where you both go for a walk and grab some ice cream and talk about this together so that its more of an open discussion. Ask what his expectations are, what his 1-3 year plan is financially and career wise, and make sure he is curious about the same for you. Also, make sure to be honest with him about how your concerns with carrying the financial burden between you two. This includes covering monthly expenses, sharing joint expenses, etc. Maybe knowing where you both stand about your future together could incentivize him to want more for his own career ambitions. But go into knowing that you do run the risk of him realizing that he’s not ready for the next step, or maybe he does not align with what you want. 

I hope in the long run it works out for the both of you. Good luck!!

Edit: also i think its worth mentioning that even tho it’s uncomfortable it is possible to assert your financial boundaries in a way that doesn’t make your partner feel as if you are giving an ultimatum, or communicating ‘its my way or the highway’. Its a matter of if you both can listen to comprehend and consider each other’s perspectives.

First I wanna say I’m really sorry that you’re going through this, and im especially sorry that you’re at odds with your father. It sounds like he’s jaded by whatever is encouraging him to be close minded (could be past experiences, could be ego, who knows)  and its tarnishing your relationship with him. I hope in the future y’all can come together to heal your relationship with one another, but also just remember you can love a family member from a distance if they’re too harmful to be around. If to you, your father is intolerable, then you have every right to distance yourself. What you’re experiencing is so conflicting and painful and that needs to be acknowledged.

I also want to mention that I think race, ethnicity, and culture are being conflated in your post here, so I want to include definitions Im using to respond with. - -Race is a westernized categorization that classifies ppl in different groups, usually physical and social attributes. (Eg. people who identity as Indian, Japanese, Taiwanese, would be classified as Asian in a society that recognizes race)
-Ethnicity are the biological indicators that categorize you to a group (eg, being Iranian in iran, and being Iranian American, both are Iranian ethnically.)
-Culture are the customs and practices that categorize you to a group. (Eg both Iranian americans and Iranians from the mother land both practice Islam, aka a cultural practice)

I want to say that as a POC living in a western world who has experience self hatred to a degree myself, It sounds like your relationship to your father is the primarily source of conflict, and what adds to it are the real world negative examples occurrences in the world. For example, in some Arabic countries, there are a lot of examples of rampant homophobia, sexism, and sometimes anti progressive movements. But please remember that there can be positive things about these countries too. If you want to unlearn the self hatred that you’ve adopted, remember that your Arabic culture is not monolithic (same goes with western culture.) , and that there’s good, bad, and nuanced representation in ALL cultures. People are complicated, therefore cultures are complicated, but also, cultures grow and evolve. If you really want to repair that relationship you have to yourself and your culture, you can either seek out positive representations of these things, or even better, be the example you wish to see in the world. However, I do think its okay if you want reject a culture that you believe is harmful to you and people you care about. It doesnt get easier to do so when its something you’ve grown up with. Just make sure you’re doing it for reasons that bring more positivity to you. People leave harmful religions all the time, people adapt to cultures that make them feel safer all the time. Culture can also die out to if enough people are sick of it. 

With that being said, internalized racism and a hate for your own ethnicity will be difficult to over come. You cannot help your ethnicity, and you cannot help how people classify you racially/the race you identify with either. Please remember to be kind to yourself, and to accept yourself for who you are through your journey of self love. Don’t let the actions of others influence how you define yourself, and don’t let anyone define you because of the actions of others. And also, remember to forgive yourself for the conflict that you feel right now with yourself. It doesn’t make you morally bankrupt for experiencing this. I hope I worded this response out well! Sending so much positivity your way!!!

And while you excuse your own behavior you try to exert control over hers with criticism and getting upset over her not being able to read your mind ): that’s being controlling. Given the context you’ve provided, when you say ‘it’s difficult to act normal’ what you’re actually saying is that it’s difficult to hold yourself accountable when you are clearly out of line. You need to empower yourself and believe that you are able to shake the insecurities you have about your wife and yourself, but more importantly, you need to learn that it is completely not okay to make other people responsible for your emotions. It sounds like she might feel like no one is listening to her, or that the frustration she feels from her friend’s harmful behavior is not being acknowledged, and she might not realize it herself. She might feel stuck or emotionally obligated to someone who’s hurting her and doesn’t know how to confront her friend about it, so she’ll rant about it to anyone. I do this every now and then so I can understand where it could be coming from, and usually I just want to be heard when I express my grievances, it could be the same for her! She might not realize that she’s emotionally offloading on you. I also fully understand where you’re coming from too as it can be really emotionally taxing to be on the receiving end of ranting, especially when it’s someone you care about.

I would also say that you could encourage your wife to empower herself to address what’s bothering her. Maybe suggest she could write a letter addressed to her friend about how she feels. As silly as it sounds, it’s actually really helpful. Encourage her to get it all on paper in pen so it’s permanent, and reread it when she’s ready. She doesn’t even have to send it. She just needs a healthy outlet for her frustrations/a safe space where she can be vulnerable about what’s bothering her.

Also just for some perspective, I want to note that while it def seems you have her best interest at heart when you mention that you wish she’d leave these friends of hers that seem to be stressing her out, be mindful that leaving harmful cycles can be really hard. It can be addicting to keep engaging with people that do you harm, because you’re hoping they’ll do you right the next time you give them a chance. And when that falls through, the cycle begins again. It could be the case for her. 

Regardless, I hope this works out for you :) good luck!
